title: DNS Lookup: how it works, formula and examples

content:
The [DNS Lookup](/dns-lookup) is a free online tool on CalcHub. Look up DNS records for any domain — A, AAAA, MX, TXT, NS and more. Enter your domain and record type and the result appears straight away — no account or download needed. Because it runs entirely in your browser, the values you type never leave your device, and you can use it as often as you like.

Look up DNS records for any domain: A records (IPv4 addresses), AAAA (IPv6), MX (mail servers), TXT (verification and policy records), NS (name servers), CNAME (aliases) and SOA (the zone's authority record). The lookup runs over DNS-over-HTTPS against Google's public resolver, so the answer is the live public record. It is the first step in debugging “the site is down” or “email is not arriving” — if the record is wrong or missing here, it is wrong or missing everywhere. Nothing is stored.

## How to use the DNS Lookup

Start by typing or pasting your domain, then choosing your record type from the list. The result updates as you type, so adjust any value and watch the answer change. If the answer is not what you expected, check the value you entered first — a missing digit or a wrong unit is the usual cause.

1. Type a domain, like example.com.
2. Pick the record type you need.
3. Run the lookup — the records, their TTLs and the record type appear below.

## How it works

The [DNS Lookup](/dns-lookup) works straight from the values you enter: change an input and the result updates immediately, with no page reload and no waiting. Everything happens in your browser, so your entries never leave your device. Try it with a few different values and you will quickly get a feel for how the inputs move the result.

## Worked example

Here is a typical example. Looking up example.com's A records returns its IPv4 addresses with their TTLs; its MX records show which servers handle its mail. Try the same figures in the [DNS Lookup](/dns-lookup) and you will get the same result — then change one value at a time to see how the answer moves.

## Trying it out

The fastest way to see what the [DNS Lookup](/dns-lookup) does is to open it and enter values you already know the answer for. Change one input at a time and watch how the result responds — that tells you more than any description. Everything runs in your browser, so you can experiment freely: nothing is saved, sent or tracked.

## What the record types mean

A points a name at an IPv4 address; AAAA at an IPv6 address. MX names the servers that accept mail for the domain, in priority order. TXT carries text — SPF, DKIM and domain verification strings live here. NS names the domain's name servers. CNAME makes one name an alias of another. SOA holds the zone's serial number and timers, including how long negative answers are cached.

## Why lookups differ

DNS answers are cached, so a change you made an hour ago may not show everywhere yet — the TTL on each record says how long it can be cached. Different resolvers can also answer differently during that window. If this tool shows the new record, the change has propagated to public resolvers; if not, wait out the old TTL.

## Tips

A few things worth knowing before you rely on the result — most of them are about the numbers you put in, rather than the tool itself:

- “No records of this type” usually means the record does not exist, not that the tool failed.
- Check MX records first when email stops arriving.
- The TTL tells you how long a cached answer can linger after a change.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is a DNS lookup?

A query of the Domain Name System for a domain's records: which IP address it points to (A/AAAA), which servers handle its mail (MX), and the rest. This tool asks Google's public resolver over HTTPS. Try it with your own numbers in the [DNS Lookup](/dns-lookup) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### Why does my domain show no MX records?

Either the domain has no mail set up, or the records were added recently and have not propagated yet. Check the spelling and try again in a few minutes. Try it with your own numbers in the [DNS Lookup](/dns-lookup) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### What is a TTL?

Time To Live — how long, in seconds, a resolver may cache an answer. After a DNS change, the old answer can linger for up to the TTL. Try it with your own numbers in the [DNS Lookup](/dns-lookup) — the result updates as you type, so you can test a few scenarios in seconds.

### What do I need to use the DNS Lookup?

Just Domain and Record type. Enter those values and the result appears straight away — no account or download needed. If you are unsure about a value, try a rough figure first and then refine it — the result updates instantly.
